blocks.text: 14th October 2026 - Link Blog

AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary. (via) Indie game developer Popcar talks about the recent wave of AI-powered decompilation of existing games, enabling weird mashups between existing games, and producing a boom in game preservation projects to get old games working on new hardware (often in a browser using WebAssembly).
I like how this piece captures both the positives and the negatives of this new development:

Most people already realized the scary part by now. If AI can decompile games and software, then the entire tech industry is about to explode. Anybody can decompile other software and use it any way they'd like, and nobody can stop them. Companies can steal from competitors. Your paid game or app can be open-sourced against your will. This isn't exclusive to old video games, we can apply this to any software. [...]
This is also a big win for preservation. Old games can be ported, modified, enhanced, and made much more easily accessible than before.  [...[
With console makers going all in on digital and games becoming entirely unplayable due to servers shutting down, this is fantastic news. We could own software we bought regardless of what the company thinks.
13th October 2026 - Link Blog

Redesigning source control at Anthropic (via) Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months.
In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day.
They included a chart showing those changes. I had Claude modify their chart (code here) to add markers for the public releases of each of their models in 2026:

This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity.

"Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion. They had some pretty extreme requirements:

The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day.
The new system was built by a team of seven people, and the migration from Git was completed in five months.
When asked on Hacker News about the lack of offline support, Scion engineer Nick G replied:
Since Claude is by far the heaviest user of Scion and is necessarily online, this just wasn't important to do.

As an aside, I've been trying adversarial review in my own projects recently, where you have a model try and find flaws (I often play Claude and GPT off against each other). This note from the article reflected my own experience with that:

Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Claude away from over-engineering parts of the system in response to hypothetical concerns.

blocks.text: I added support to llm-gemini for the new Gemini 4 Argon model, made available today via the Gemini API and for customers of their $100/month subscription plan.

Here are the low, medium and high pelicans. As expected, they are all excellent: Gemini has a track record of producing great SVGs, and are the only lab where I know their staff have invested in SVG specifically (and who have boasted about their pelicans before.)
Here's the "high" illustration, which cost me 17.166 cents:

The pricing is interesting. At launch, Argon is $2/million input and $10/million output - the same price as GPT-6 Sol, half the price of Claude Opus 5.5 and 1/5th the price of Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra.
But on December 1st Argon is set to double in price - so it will be the same price as Opus 5.5.
Prices like this aren't really comparable these days since what really matters is how many tokens a model takes to achieve a goal within an agentic harness.

One useful clue for that comes from Artificial Analysis, who publish the total cost to run their benchmark using each model. Argon is looking very good there - costing $2,407 to run the benchmark, putting it close to GLM-5.3 and significantly cheaper than OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta's latest models.
When the price doubles it will still be a little cheaper than GPT-6 Astra.
(I used ChatGPT to edit that chart! The data is all correct, I checked - I needed to get that Gemini 4 Argon info box to display without overlapping the other numbers.)

Some bonus examples using Gemini 4 Argon: here's Generate an SVG of an armadillo in fishnet tights jaywalking on Mars, here's a Fabergé egg it created for me using Blender, and DeepMind staffer @fofrAI shared a video of a pelican riding a bike, using fourier epicycles. That's a fun new twist!

articles.title: Formlabs dropped the Raspberry Pi on the way to a $699 SLA printer
articles.titleZh: Formlabs dropped the Raspberry Pi on the way to a $699 SLA printer
articles.summary: Formlabs dropped the Raspberry Pi on the way to a $699 SLA printer

blocks.text: Formlabs sent me a Form Studio 1 resin 3D printer to test after years of back-and-forth about their Form 4 printer.

Like the Form 4, it's an SLA (stereolithography) printer, but unlike the Form 4 (which starts at $2,600), it's affordable for a hobbyist. It's not cheap, coming in at $699 (or $749 with a flex build platform, which I highly recommend), but it is affordable.

I can't say as much about this printer as people who are well-versed in resin printing and use other SLA printers (all my experience until now is with FDM, or Fused Deposition Modeling1, printers). But I can convey my first-time experience using this printer and with the entire SLA experience.

It's a more tedious process, which involves resins you can't touch, multiple gallons of IPA (Isopropyl Alcohol) for washing, and curing in UV light... but the end result has a resolution that can't be matched with FDM, and materials ranging from clear resin to flexible rubber are equally unreal to see come off the printer if you’re only used to filament printers.

Besides the tedious post-processing, resin (at least on the consumer level) can't do multi-color/multi-material prints—something that's become almost commonplace on filament printers this year, and has its own interesting use cases.

But I printed a number of items, including the one I was most excited to try—GutBomb's MacPicoModem enclosure, but clear, and with the traditional speaker hump that is iconic on Global Village modems for old Macs.
Anyway, I posted my full experience, and a review of the Form Studio 1, in today's video on YouTube:

Formlabs also provided this link to the Form Studio 1 that tracks where people visit from, but I don't participate in their affiliate program (I only participate in Amazon Affiliates). They are selling four 'special edition' colored plastic versions for a limited time, and I only wish those were permanent options (only grey will be permanent).

The video above goes into a few more details about their value engineering, as well—it takes a lot to go from $2,600 down to $700—and I even had the honor of speaking to KRALYN (who built the Positron, and headed the Studio 1 project) about how they tackled a number of engineering challenges.

One of the more interesting nuggets was their decision to drop the Raspberry Pi Compute Module (used in the Form 4). The Studio 1 adopts a different Arm SoM, and that meant more work building a proper camera driver (Raspberry Pi's camera stack just worked out of the box), and going through the wireless certification process (Pi CMs are pre-certified if using their approved antennas). But apparently it was worth it for the cost savings.

Between that, reducing the power output of the UV light, using a cheaper plastic hinge instead of the metal damped hinge on the Form 4, and dropping the mixing arm that is more necessary for higher-end resins (some costing $300+ per liter!), they were able to get the cost a little south of $1,000.

There are other SLA resin printers for half the cost, and some other resins that are cheaper than Formlabs' own, too. I can't speak to reliability or quality versus those printers, but at least having hardware under a grand means Formlabs can address a new audience—people like me, who had a hard time justifying a Form 4. Especially since 'Open Material Mode' is free2 on this printer—it's a $875 addon for the Form 4!
The type of 3D printer that extrudes filament through a tiny hot end. ↩︎
It requires use of the Form Studio Resin Tank Pro ($79), which is $24 more expensive than the standard Form Studio Resin Tank ($55). ↩︎

articles.title: U.K. Sanctions Cryptomus for RU Money Laundering
articles.titleZh: U.K. Sanctions Cryptomus for RU Money Laundering
articles.summary: U.K. Sanctions Cryptomus for RU Money Laundering

blocks.text: The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.
Heleket’s support agent on Telegram claims, despite all evidence to the contrary, that it is not affiliated with Cryptomus. Image: Richard Sanders.

On October 8, the U.K. issued sanctions (PDF) against Cryptomus — previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises — for processing payments that benefit the Russian government and its financial institutions. The sanctions freeze any Cryptomus assets at U.K. banks, and bar British companies from offering it any business, virtual or otherwise. Also targeted in these sanctions were the virtual payment platforms VexPay, TokenSpot, and the Tsunami Payments service.

As explained in our December 2024 investigation, “How Cryptocurrency Turns to Cash in Russian Banks,” Cryptomus has been a key payment processor for dozens of Russian cryptocurrency exchanges and websites hawking cybercrime services. The company has changed its name several times since emerging in 2022, most recently to “Heleket” last year after Canada levied a record CAD $176 million fine against the platform for anti-money laundering violations.
The blockchain data-crunching firm Chainalysis said the U.K. sanctions target the broader infrastructure supporting Russia’s wartime economy.

“Cryptomus and Heleket have emerged as major payment hubs for illicit activity,” Chainalysis wrote in an October 8 blog post. “Together, these services received more illicit funds across tracked categories than the mixers in our dataset and the number of illicit counterparties surged to more than 900 in a single month in late 2025.”
The Cryptomus support bot on Telegram, responding on Oct. 8 to an inquiry by saying the platform was suddenly unable to process transactions.

In April 2026, the blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs found Cryptomus had processed more than $7 billion in transactions since its inception in 2022, including transactions associated with child sexual abuse material vendors, terrorist financing networks, and human trafficking operations.

TRM noted that Cryptomus’s transaction volume cratered after the platform instituted new “know your customer” or KYC rules, and that the cryptocurrency platform responded to the Canadian fines by launching Heleket as a parallel service that continued to offer no-KYC payment processing.

Richard Sanders is a blockchain analyst and investigator who spent months mapping out Cryptomus’s payment infrastructure and transacting with its customers. Sanders said the U.K. sanctions on Cryptomus are important because Canada’s sanctions against the platform were ultimately unenforceable and uncollectible.
“A fine doesn’t stop a cryptocurrency payment processor from processing payments,” Sanders wrote on LinkedIn. “Sanctions kill the operation. The distinction matters.”

As our 2024 investigation noted, Cryptomus shared a Vancouver address with dozens of other foreign currency dealers and money transfer businesses — none of which appeared to be physically located there. Following the CAD $176 million fine for alleged money laundering violations, Cryptomus appealed the penalty, launched Heleket as a parallel service, and kept on processing large volumes of sketchy transactions, Sanders said.

Sanders said the sanctions also are notable because they are the first known instance of a “Five Eyes” country (referring to the Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the U.K. and the U.S.) sanctioning a cryptocurrency operation incorporated in another Five Eyes jurisdiction.

Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation.

Our 2024 investigation found the sole shareholder of Cryptomus’s parent company Certa Payments was a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman who also headed several other firms, including the WS Management and Advisory Corporation, which bills itself as the regulatory body that exclusively oversees licenses for cryptocurrency, foreign exchange and online gaming businesses incorporated in the disputed region in northwest Africa known as the Western Sahara.

That entity’s website — crasadr.com — says it assists applicants with bank setup and formation, online gaming licenses, and the creation and licensing of foreign exchange brokers. One of Certa Payments’ former sites — certa[.]website — also shared a server with 12 other domains, including rasd-state[.]ws, a website for the Central Reserve Authority of the Western Sahara.

The website crasadr dot com, the official website of the Central Reserve Authority of Western Sahara, which lists the entities awarded licenses for cryptocurrencies, gaming and foreign exchange services.

articles.title: Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws
articles.titleZh: Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws
articles.summary: Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws

blocks.text: Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.

Just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions.

Windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. A few months ago, Microsoft quietly extended that support for another year (until October 2027).

At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an attacker to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system.

While Microsoft said there are no signs anyone is exploiting it yet, a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework (CVE-2026-108398) was publicly disclosed prior to today, potentially giving attackers advance time to work out how to exploit the bug.
Satnam Narang at Tenable said the number of flaws fixed this month far surpasses the previous record-setting year 2020, when Microsoft patched 1,261 CVEs.
“We’ve now crossed the 4,000 CVE mark with two months left to go,” he said.

Microsoft credits large language models for the high volume of bug discovery, and presumably AI gets credit for many of the patches used to fix these flaw. Meanwhile, security experts have been warning that these unusually large patch volleys from Microsoft are placing extra strain on corporate security teams, which often have to test individual updates before deploying them across a network to ensure the fixes don’t cause problems for other software.

Tyler Reguly, associate director of security research and development at Fortra, notes that just 26 Microsoft vulnerabilities appeared in the “Known Exploited Vulnerabilities” (KEV) catalog maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) so far this year, and security teams would do well to prioritize patching those 26 vulnerabilities first.
“Security leaders should focus on exploitable risk, and ask whether their teams have the clarity, capacity and support to act,” Reguly said.

Which vulnerabilities deserve the most scrutiny in your organization? The folks at Cisco Talos have a useful roundup of the more noteworthy flaws that Microsoft fixed today, and of course the SANS Internet Storm Center has a reliable roundup that indexes vulnerabilities by severity, CVE number and affected software.

articles.title: The Internet of Very Cheap Things
articles.titleZh: The Internet of Very Cheap Things
articles.summary: The Internet of Very Cheap Things

blocks.text: Twelve years ago, I was complaining that IoT devices were too expensive.  Last week I bought a colour changing Zigbee lighbulb for £4. Not a typo - less than a fiver.
While the aipocalypse is devouring RAM with its insatiable appetite, Moore's Law appears to be keeping up its end of the bargain when it comes to domestic gadgetry.

This blog posts compares today's prices with those from a little over a decade ago. Some of the changes are startling, others less so. I'm basing the prices on what a customer can easily get today from Amazon. Yes, AliExpress is cheaper - but delivery takes and age and returns are a faff. Also, I get delicious affiliate revenue when you click the links which allows me to buy more tech crap to review. Everyone's a winner!
Door / Window Sensors

I don't know how many doors and windows you have in your property - we have about fifteen, not including internal doors and cupboards. Back then a single sensor cost around £30. Today you can get Zigbee door sensors for between £15 - £30 for a pack of four!

Prices are at least quartered. Do you need a sensor on every cupboard door or drawer? It is useful to be able to check your phone to see if the toilet seat is up or down? These are reaching the price where you might as well hook them up to anything.
Lightbulbs
Hue's WiFi lightbulbs were about fifty-quid each. Again, count the number of lights you need in your home and run to your bank-manager for an overdraft!

Today, Hue Bulbs are about £16 each. That's a pretty steep drop. If you want generic Zigbee Bulbs you can expect to pay a tenner each. That's down to a fifth of the price from 2014. If you're happy buying from AliExpress, they're usually under a fiver.
Smart Electrical Sockets

It's useful to be able to remotely control a power socket. It used to be the case they'd cost £30 per plug. Nowadays smart plugs are about £7.50. These ones come with energy monitoring and will easily integrate with HomeAssistant and other smarthome controllers.
There's still a limit to the things which can be directly controlled from a socket. That said, I'm love my IoT Electric Blanket.
Bluetooth Finders

The dream is to have a magic tag stuck on everything you might lose. Back in 2014, we thought iBeacons / Eddystones would win out. Sadly that dream died and instead we're stuck with proprietary "Find My" networks from Google and Apple.

The iBeacons were about a tenner each back then. Today they're £5 - £10 each depending on the features you want. That's still not cheap enough to attach to every sock - but there's no excuse for losing your keys, wallet, bag, or spouse again.
Annoyingly they don't use an open standard, so you'll need a Google or Apple account to use them.

I still prefer QR codes (free!) to NFC, but I concede they do have their uses. Their capacity and features are much the same as they were a decade ago, but prices have dropped from about 75p per tag down to about 10p-20p per tag.
At that price, it's just about cheap enough to stick them in every book you own or sew them into all your underpants. Quite why you'd want to do that is left as an exercise for the reader.
Internet Fridge

You know what, I didn't bother looking at the actual cost of an Internet Fridge all those years ago. But earlier this year I got a WiFi enabled tumble dryer. It was as cheap as all the other models and means I can shout "ALEXA! MAKE DRY!" then receive a notification from HomeAssistant when the dry is fully maked.
I hope my next fridge comes with a sensor that alerts me if the door is left open or the freezer is getting too warm. That would be handy.
The cost of an ESP32 is basically a rounding error for most large appliances, especially when bought in bulk. If it uses electricity, it is probably trivial to add WiFi and Bluetooth.
What's Next?

There's probably a realistic limit to how low prices can go while the products still remain safe and durable. For smaller items that appears to be between a fiver in bulk direct from China to about a tenner sourced from a mainstream UK supplier.
For domestic appliances, there doesn't seem to be any significant extra cost. Take a look at these heat pump tumble dryers - even the cheapest of them comes with an app.
There are a few bits of my home which haven't yet been given their own IP address - although they're mostly towards the mechanical side of things.

Locks
							
								There are some 
									smart-locks for doors. I've not seen any for windows. I'm not sure how well I'd trust their security.

While the aipocalypse is devouring RAM with its insatiable appetite, Moore's Law appears to be keeping up its end of the bargain when it comes to domestic gadgetry.

This blog posts compares today's prices with those from a little over a decade ago. Some of the changes are startling, others less so. I'm basing the prices on what a customer can easily get today from Amazon. Yes, AliExpress is cheaper - but delivery takes and age and returns are a faff. Also, I get delicious affiliate revenue when you click the links which allows me to buy more tech crap to review. Everyone's a winner!
Door / Window Sensors

I don't know how many doors and windows you have in your property - we have about fifteen, not including internal doors and cupboards. Back then a single sensor cost around £30. Today you can get Zigbee door sensors for between £15 - £30 for a pack of four!

Prices are at least quartered. Do you need a sensor on every cupboard door or drawer? It is useful to be able to check your phone to see if the toilet seat is up or down? These are reaching the price where you might as well hook them up to anything.
Lightbulbs
Hue's WiFi lightbulbs were about fifty-quid each. Again, count the number of lights you need in your home and run to your bank-manager for an overdraft!

Today, Hue Bulbs are about £16 each. That's a pretty steep drop. If you want generic Zigbee Bulbs you can expect to pay a tenner each. That's down to a fifth of the price from 2014. If you're happy buying from AliExpress, they're usually under a fiver.
Smart Electrical Sockets

It's useful to be able to remotely control a power socket. It used to be the case they'd cost £30 per plug. Nowadays smart plugs are about £7.50. These ones come with energy monitoring and will easily integrate with HomeAssistant and other smarthome controllers.
There's still a limit to the things which can be directly controlled from a socket. That said, I'm love my IoT Electric Blanket.
Bluetooth Finders

The dream is to have a magic tag stuck on everything you might lose. Back in 2014, we thought iBeacons / Eddystones would win out. Sadly that dream died and instead we're stuck with proprietary "Find My" networks from Google and Apple.

The iBeacons were about a tenner each back then. Today they're £5 - £10 each depending on the features you want. That's still not cheap enough to attach to every sock - but there's no excuse for losing your keys, wallet, bag, or spouse again.
Annoyingly they don't use an open standard, so you'll need a Google or Apple account to use them.

I still prefer QR codes (free!) to NFC, but I concede they do have their uses. Their capacity and features are much the same as they were a decade ago, but prices have dropped from about 75p per tag down to about 10p-20p per tag.
At that price, it's just about cheap enough to stick them in every book you own or sew them into all your underpants. Quite why you'd want to do that is left as an exercise for the reader.

You know what, I didn't bother looking at the actual cost of an Internet Fridge all those years ago. But earlier this year I got a WiFi enabled tumble dryer. The cost of an ESP32 is basically a rounding error for most large appliances, especially when bought in bulk. If it uses electricity, it is probably trivial to add WiFi and Bluetooth.
What's Next?

There's probably a realistic limit to how low prices can go while the products still remain safe and durable. For smaller items that appears to be between a fiver in bulk direct from China to about a tenner sourced from a mainstream UK supplier.
For domestic appliances, there doesn't seem to be any significant extra cost. Take a look at these heat pump tumble dryers - even the cheapest of them comes with an app.

blocks.text: G. D. Chakerian [1] discovered the following generalization of the Pythagorean theorem.

Take any triangle and attach squares to each side. From each triangle vertex, extend a line perpendicular to the opposite side and extend the line through the square, as shown in the figure below. Then the areas of the rectangles with the same labels are equal.
It’s not clear at first why this is a generalization of the Pythagorean theorem, but if we make our triangle closer to a right triangle it’s easier to see the connection.

As the angle at B becomes closer to a right angle, the area of the orange triangles labeled II goes to zero. In the limit we’re left a theorem saying that the areas of the blue and green squares add up to the area of the square attached to the hypotenuse.

The paper [1] caught my eye because it gives a connection between a geometry problem and a circuit problem, much like this post. However, I find the theorem itself more interesting than the connection to circuits.
The first diagram is my reproduction of the first figure from the paper, with color added. I then moved the vertex A to make the connection to the Pythagorean theorem easier to see.
Related posts
Four generalizations of the Pythagorean theorem
Sparse binary Pythagorean triples
Napoleon’s theorem
[1] G. D. Chakerian and M. S. Klamkin. A Generalization of the Pythagorean Theorem Seen as a Problem of Equivalent Resistances. Mathematics Magazine, Vol. 59, No. 3 (Jun., 1986), pp. 149–153.

The first line of the paper is “The following result (observed several years ago by the first author) may be viewed as a generalization of the Pythagorean Theorem.” The paper also gives two other sources of the theorem. Presumably Chakerian independently discovered a theorem that was already known.

blocks.text: What’s a connection between Edgar Allan Poe and Friedrich Wilhelm Bessel?

Poe’s story The Pit and the Pendulum describes a pendulum with a semicircular blade being lowered on a cable. This is an interesting variation on the usual harmonic oscillator because the length L of the pendulum is not constant but rather an increasing function of time L(t).
Using the small angle approximation sin(θ) ≈ θ, the equation of motion is
L θ″ + L′ θ′ + g θ = 0.

If we assume the length is increasing at a constant rate, then with a change of variables described in [1], this differential equation becomes Bessel’s equation and its solutions are Bessel functions.
The authors of [1] state that their primary interest is whether a pendulum can have the motion that Poe describes. But as they indicate in their opening sentence,
The study of the motion of a steadily descending pendulum has practical applications (e.g., to the oscillations of a load being lowered by a crane).
A more recent application would be describing the motion of a package being delivered by a Zipline drone.
Related posts
Pi and The Raven
The nonlinear pendulum equation
From Kepler to Bessel
[1] Robert L. Borrelli, Courtney S. Coleman, and Dana D. Hobson. Poe’s Pendulum. Mathematics Magazine, Vol. 58, No. 2 (Mar., 1985), pp. 78–83
On October 14, 2009, SCO fired its CEO, Darl McBride. Very nearly 15 years later, McBride died at the age of 64 of complications from ALS.

His termination from SCO ended his time as the most hated man in technology. McBride architected SCO’s Business strategy of suing companies for contributing code to Linux, or even for using Linux. He spent the rest of his life trying to fight his way back from relative obscurity to reach a similar height.
Darl McBride’s business model

SCO was one of dozens of companies who licensed the operating system Unix and produced commercial products based on the original Unix code. In SCO’s case, they had been a subcontractor to Microsoft to help Microsoft produce their own version of Unix, originally called Xenix. When Microsoft decided to get out of that business, they sold the product back to SCO, who continued to market the product on its own. If you wanted to run Unix on commodity Intel based PC hardware, you bought one of SCO’s products. It was cheaper to buy a Compaq and run SCO on it than to buy a Unix workstation from Sun Microsystems or Silicon Graphics.

Dozens of other companies licensed the Unix code to build operating systems for their own proprietary hardware. There were any number of reasons why someone might want to do that. Early on, the hardware reached levels of performance and/or reliability that Intel couldn’t match. Later on as Intel moved upmarket, the decision was frequently driven by software. There would be some piece of software a company needed, support was available on some number of these platforms, and they selected the one they were most comfortable with.

Linux gradually wore away at this business model. Over the course of the 1990s, proprietary Unix vendors reacted to the threat using different methods. Two of them, Silicon Graphics and IBM, decided they were better off joining them than trying to compete with free. They started contributing code and helping to mature the operating system.
SCO took a somewhat different approach. They sued IBM.
SCO v. IBM

SCO and IBM had a bit of a history. They had cooperated on a product called Project Monterey starting in 1998. In 2001, IBM had a change of heart, decided the last thing the post-Linux world really needed was yet another proprietary Unix, and changed direction.

After filing suit, SCO painted a word picture of Linux as a bicycle and its own product as a sports car. And they said IBM willfully undermined SCO’s business by turning Linux into a sports car, including contributing copyrighted code.

Problem was, the code that SCO said infringed their copyrights had been previously released under an open source license or contributed into the public domain. SCO couldn’t claim ownership of it. Furthermore, it wasn’t even IBM who had contributed the code. It had been Silicon Graphics who did it.

Here’s a word picture for you. I stand 5’9″ and weigh about 150 pounds.  That’s about 175cm and 70kg for those of you who use metric. I’m not a big guy. Now imagine little and dainty me accusing John Cena of something he didn’t do. And then taking a swing at him. And having an attitude about it.
It’s possible John Cena would give the yappy little runt whatever it wanted so it would go away. But it’s also safe to say a Marine turned professional wrestler has other options.
Suffice it to say, IBM didn’t pay SCO to make it go away. IBM beat SCO to within an inch of its life and let it live.
As for the Linux project, its maintainers shored up the code vetting process to prevent a repeat occurrence. So far that’s been pretty successful.

In 2021, SCO sold its intellectual property to Xinuous and renamed itself to TSG Group. In August 2021, TSG Group settled with IBM for $14.25 million as part of its bankruptcy proceedings. Xinuous, meanwhile, continued the ancient litigation, and on August 10, 2026, the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit ruled it was too late to re-litigate the matter. Xinuous announced its intent to appeal before the full bench of the court, something that only succeeds 0.03 percent of the time. So it is likely that the matter of SCO v. IBM did eventually close, after a quarter century.
SCO v. Chrysler

The other notorious lawsuit brought about by Darl McBride’s business plan was against Chrysler. Years before, in 1988, Chrysler had purchased a Cray supercomputer, and they wanted to run Unix on it. So they purchased a license for Unix, which they presumably handed over to some IT integrator, who in turn configured their Cray supercomputer for them.

Like any computer, Chrysler’s Cray had a finite useful life expectancy, and it is entirely possible, even likely, that by the time SCO came calling in 2003, that Cray had been decommissioned and parts of it were sitting in somebody’s basement. It had an integrated padded bench, so it would make a great trophy that can double as a couch.
In December 2003, SCO sent Chrysler a letter demanding an accounting of any and all use of Unix and Linux in the company. Chrysler never responded, so SCO sued them in March 2004.

It turned out Chrysler probably never even received the letter, because it had changed ownership and moved, and SCO mailed the letter to an office building that no longer had anything to do with Chrysler.

Linux users didn’t take kindly to this. In an era when the RIAA was suing 12-year-olds and working class mothers sharing boy-band MP3s, many of them wondered if SCO was going to turn to suing them as a business model. They couldn’t afford to put up a fight the way Chrysler or IBM could.

This business model failed to produce revenue but proved very effective at generating a great deal of ill will. By 2009, SCO had enough and fired the architect of the business model, although curiously, they continued the lawsuit with IBM. One would think they would eventually cut their losses.

After SCO, McBride kept a fairly low profile. He got into the mobile app business as CEO of Shout, but largely stayed out of the public eye, which was probably the right decision. Shout was acquired by MMA Global in 2018, and McBride left the combined company in 2021, after filing for personal bankruptcy in December 2020. He then went to work at VirnetX, a Japanese holding company that appears to specialize in highly secure video conferencing.
Spinning McBride’s tenure at SCO

In a paywalled 2015 interview with the San Jose Business Journal, McBride said, “I’ve had some great wins but also some tough times. I believe the adage ‘The best form of revenge is success.’ Go after it and stay focused. If you strike out, go back to the basics and start over again.”

His LinkedIn page doesn’t try to hide his time at SCO, spinning it as a troubled company lying to its executive candidate about its financial condition and how much time he really had to turn the company around. He also claimed he didn’t know about the dispute with IBM when he started. That’s because he started the dispute, against the advice of his predecessor, Ransom Love. Love said as much in the Feb 2, 2004 issue of Businessweek.

McBride’s profile also included a diatribe about how IBM lured Linux developers into bullying him. That’s also spin. Linux developers went on the offensive against McBride because they didn’t want to get sued too, and they believed the best defense is a good offense.

His obituary spun his time at SCO defiantly: “A full-page photo of Darl commanded the cover of Fortune magazine’s May 2004 issue when he was the CEO of SCO Corporation, and considered a modern-day David at battle with business Goliaths including IBM.”

I’m familiar with the story of David and Goliath. As I recall, David won. There’s also the small matter of David being the good guy. McBride lost and wasn’t the good guy. So I don’t know anyone who considered Darl McBride a modern-day David-and-Goliath story, but maybe I just haven’t met enough people. I’m pretty introverted.

For whatever it’s worth, SCO’s predecessor company, Caldera, suing Microsoft and getting $280 million is closer to my idea of a David-and-Goliath story. But that was before Darl McBride’s time. He was working for a startup called Pointserve when that was going on. But my theory is McBride took inspiration from the Caldera suit and thought IBM would fold the way Microsoft folded for Caldera. But Microsoft was fighting antitrust battles IBM wasn’t fighting. So instead, McBride learned why Gary Kildall feared IBM.
Darl McBride’s death
Darl McBride died September 16, 2024 of complications from ALS, also known as Lou Gehrig’s disease. ALS is a terrible way to go, so I hope McBride somehow found peace.

It took a few years, but McBride went from being the most hated man in tech to mostly forgotten. I didn’t see any mention of his death on any of the tech news sites when it happened. Closer to 2009, it would have been big news. An old Russian joke about obituaries comes to mind. Obituaries aren’t on the front page. But this one would have been, at least on the tech sites.
